title: Control Flow
subtitle: The Ley Clock Decides
martuIntro:
The Ley Clock does not panic. It checks. If the hand is near the arc, it warns. Otherwise, it waits.
Today you teach Python to check the same way. And you learn to roll dice, because the world is not fair, yes?
You have seen this code already: the four dialogue options, the trap-door skill checks. It felt like a wall. Now we take it apart, one stone at a time.
goals: Ask yes-or-no questions with `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`, and get `True` or `False`
Choose `>=` on purpose, so exactly enough still passes
Compare text exactly, and with `.lower()` so capitals don't matter
Write `if`, `else` and `elif` with colons and indents, knowing the first true branch wins
Roll dice with `import random` and `random.randint(1, 20)`, both ends included
Read Python's error message, find the line, and mend it

items.title: Quick review: 2 questions (not scored)
items.summary: Two quick questions from Unit 1, to warm up. Nothing is scored.

questions.q: What will this line show in the Console?
questions.explain: `*` repeats text, like a stamp pressed again and again: `"█" * 2` is `██`, and `"░" * 3` is `░░░`. Then `+` glues the two together, with no space between.

questions.q: Rope is sold by the coil (one roll of rope). In `rope_count * rope_price`, which box is *how many* coils?

whyWrong.1: `rope_price` is how much one coil costs. `rope_count` is how many coils you buy.

questions.explain: Cost = how many × the price of one, like unit price in math class. `rope_count` is how many, and `rope_price` is the price of one.

exercises.title: True or False
exercises.martu:
A [[comparison]] is a yes-or-no question about two values. Python works it out and answers [[True and False|True or False]]. In math class, you decide if 9 > 4 is true or false. Python does the same: `print(9 > 4)` shows `True`.
`>` means *more than*, and `<` means *less than*, as in math. The open side of the sign faces the bigger number.
`True` and `False` start with a capital letter and have no quotes. They are Python's own yes and no, not text.
In the code, `dex` is Bomb Shell's DEX: how quick her hands are. The latch needs 15. Guess first, then press ▶ Run, just above your code.

anotherWay.label: A light switch
anotherWay.text:
A yes-or-no answer is like a light switch: on or off, nothing in between.
```text
6 < 15   ->  [ON ]  True
6 > 15   ->  [OFF]  False
```

anotherWay.label: A yes-or-no question
anotherWay.text: "Are you taller than the door?" has only two answers: yes or no. A comparison is that kind of question. Python says `True` for yes and `False` for no.

`print(dex < needed)`:
1. Python looks inside the boxes: `6 < 15`.
2. It works out the question: is 6 less than 15? Yes.
3. It shows the answer in the Console: `True`.
A comparison is a yes-or-no question. Python answers `True` or `False`.

anotherWay.label: Why does this work? No quotes
anotherWay.text: `True` has no quotes. It is not a word to show. It is Python's own yes. `"True"` with quotes is only four letters of text, like `"glug"`.

exercises.title: Asking with ==
exercises.martu:
In Python, one `=` puts a value in a box: read it as *gets*. To ask whether two values are the same, Python uses two: `==`. Read it as [[is the same as]]. In math class, `=` says both sides are equal. `==` asks that as a question: `"owl" == "owl"` is `True`.
`!=` asks the opposite, *is not the same as*, like ≠ in math. `"owl" != "cat"` is `True`.
Line 2 reads: `clock_is_red` gets the answer to the question, is `clock_color` the same as `"red"`? Python works out the part in parentheses first. Then the answer goes in the box.

anotherWay.label: Fill or ask
anotherWay.text:
```text
is_lucky = ...
[ is_lucky ] <- answer

hero == "Lucky"
[ hero ] ? "Lucky"
```
The first line fills a box: one `=` points into it. The second only asks: two `==` put a question mark between two things.

anotherWay.label: From math class
anotherWay.text: In math class, `=` says both sides are equal. Python already uses one `=` for *gets*, so asking needs a new sign: `==`. The keyboard has no ≠ key either, so Python types it `!=`. Read `!` as *not*.

anotherWay.label: Name tag or question
anotherWay.text: Writing your name on a name tag is `=`: you put something there. Asking "Are you Lucky?" is `==`: you only want a yes or a no.

anotherWay.label: Right side first
anotherWay.text:
`is_lucky = (hero == "Lucky")`:
1. Python looks at the right side first: is `hero` the same as `"Lucky"`?
2. `hero` holds Bomb Shell, so the answer is `False`.
3. Then `is_lucky` gets that answer.
One `=` puts a value in. Two, `==`, ask a question.

exercises.title: Enough to pass
exercises.martu:
`>=` means [[at least]]: more than, or exactly the same. It is the ≥ sign from math class, typed as two keys, `>` then `=`. On a number line it is the filled dot: the number itself counts. So `9 >= 9` is `True`.
`>` is the open dot: it leaves the number itself out, so `9 > 9` is `False`. `<=` means *at most*, like ≤.
From here on, no parentheses around the question: `can_buy = coins >= price` works the same. Python asks the question first, then puts the answer in the box.
A *roll* is the number a die lands on, as in the game's trap-door skill checks. `mana` is a hero's magic power, and `cost` is what a spell uses.

anotherWay.label: A number line
anotherWay.text:
A number line, as in math class. `>=` is the filled dot: 15 counts, so the line starts on it. `>` is the open dot: 15 is left out, so the line starts right after it.
```text
          13   14   15   16   17
roll >= 15            ●=========>
roll > 15             o====>
```

anotherWay.label: Try 14, 15, 16
anotherWay.text:
```text
roll | roll > 15 | roll >= 15
 14  |  False    |  False
 15  |  False    |  True
 16  |  True     |  True
```
Only the 15 row is different. That row is exactly enough.
A 15 opens a latch that needs 15. Bomb Shell does not need 16. Exactly enough is enough.
Should exactly enough count? Use `>=`.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: In the game, the `cast_spell` steps said: use `<` and not `<=`, because a caster with exactly enough mana can still cast. `mana < cost` asked *not enough?* Here you ask the other side, *enough?*: `mana >= cost`.

campaignLink.why: You saw this line in the game, at the trap door. `roll >= required_roll` asked: is the roll at least the number needed? Its answer was `True` or `False`. A roll of exactly 15 opened a latch that needed 15.

exercises.takeaway: `>=` means *at least*: exactly enough still passes. `>` leaves the number itself out.

predict.q: The latch needs a roll of 15. What will these three lines show in the Console?
predict.explain: 14 is one short: `False`. 15 is exactly enough: `True`, because `>=` counts the number itself. 16 is more than enough: `True`. With `>`, the 15 would fail.

exercises.title: Any case, same answer
exercises.martu:
To Python, `"YES" == "yes"` is `False`: every letter and capital counts. `.lower()` fixes that. In English, you can speak to someone by name: *Lucky, pass the rope.* The dot works the same way: `answer.lower()` asks `answer` for a [[.lower()|small-letter copy]]. So `"YES".lower()` gives `"yes"`.
The dot means: ask this text to do something. The `()` at the end makes it run.
The copy is new. The text in `answer` does not change, the way a photocopy leaves the page alone.

anotherWay.label: A copy in small letters
anotherWay.text:
```text
answer         -> "YeS"
answer.lower() -> "yes"
"yes" == "yes" -> True
```
`answer` stays the same. `answer.lower()` is a new copy in small letters.

anotherWay.label: A kind librarian
anotherWay.text: Picture a librarian who doesn't care about capitals. You write HARRY or harry, and she finds the same book. `.lower()` makes Python work like that: it compares small letters with small letters.

`said_yes = answer.lower() == "yes"`:
1. `answer.lower()` makes a copy in small letters: `"yes"`.
2. Python asks: is `"yes"` the same as `"yes"`? `True`.
3. `said_yes` gets `True`.
Small letters on both sides: `answer.lower() == "yes"`.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: In the game, in Module 1, Mar'tu's dialogue line went through `.lower()` and then `.capitalize()` before it was shown. That tidied any capitals the player typed. Same dot, same idea.

exercises.title: Broken spell
exercises.martu:
This spell has three [[bug|bugs]], three mistakes in the code. Two are loud: Python stops and shows an error box in the Console. One is quiet: the code runs, but a box holds the wrong kind of thing. Each step says *Mend*, which means fix.
When Python stops, read the box in the Console in this order:
1. The title at the top says what went wrong.
2. *Python's last line* says the same thing in Python's words.
3. Find the line number. Fix that line, then press Run again.
A new error means Python got further. That's good news. Fix the next one the same way.

anotherWay.label: Which bug first?
anotherWay.text:
1. Press Run. Python stops at the first loud bug. Its error box gives the line number. Fix that line.
2. Press Run again. A new error is good news: Python got further.
3. When nothing stops, read the message under the step in Your steps.

anotherWay.label: Two kinds of bug
anotherWay.text:
```text
loud bug:
  Python stops and
  shows an error box.

quiet bug:
  the code runs, but a
  box holds the wrong
  kind of thing.
```

anotherWay.label: From English class
anotherWay.text: An error box is like a teacher's note in the margin of your draft. It points to the spot, and it isn't a grade. *Syntax* is how a sentence is put together, so a SyntaxError is a line Python can't read, like a sentence with its words in the wrong order.

hints: Press Run and read the box in the Console: first its title, then Python's last line, `SyntaxError: invalid syntax`. Both point at line 3. Look at the two marks between `roll` and `needed`.
*Syntax* means how a line is put together, like grammar in English class. Type a two-key sign in the order you say it: *greater than or equal to* is `>`, then `=`, as in `coins >= price`.
On line 3, type `>=` instead of `=>`: the `>` first, then the `=`. Line 3 becomes `passed = roll >= needed`.

whyWrong.0: `=` puts a value in a box. Read it as *gets*: `mana = 26` means mana gets 26. It asks nothing.

questions.explain: `==` asks a question. Read it as *is the same as*: `hero == "Lucky"` asks whether `hero` holds Lucky. `=` puts a value in a box.

exercises.title: If
exercises.martu:
An [[if]] line asks a yes-or-no question, like the comparisons in the last lesson. When the answer is `True`, Python runs the [[indent|indented]] lines under it. When it is `False`, Python skips them. It works like a choose-your-own-adventure book: *If you open the door, turn to page 12*. Here, `if hours_left < 3:` asks: are fewer than 3 hours left?
The `if` line ends with a [[colon]], `:`. Each line that belongs to the `if` starts with four spaces.
Try it if you like (it's not a step): press Run. Then change line 1 to `hours_left = 10` and press Run again. Why does nothing show?

anotherWay.label: A fork in the road
anotherWay.text:
```text
hours_left < 3 ?
   True  -> run the indented lines
   False -> skip them, go on
```
The `if` is a fork in the road. The answer to its question decides which way Python goes.

anotherWay.label: If it rains
anotherWay.text: If it rains, take the umbrella and wear boots. No rain? You skip both. The indented lines are the things you do only when the answer is yes.

anotherWay.label: Step table
anotherWay.text:
With `hours_left = 10`:
1. `hours_left = 10`: the box holds 10.
2. `if hours_left < 3:` asks: is 10 less than 3? `False`.
3. Python skips every indented line under the `if`.
4. Nothing shows in the Console.

anotherWay.label: The barrier door
anotherWay.text: My barrier door opens only if the hours are short. When many hours are left, the door stays shut, and the lines behind it never run.

Every indented line belongs to the `if`, like the sub-points under a main point in an outline:
```python
if rain > 0:
    print("Take the umbrella.")
    print("Wear boots.")
```
Both lines run when it rains. Neither runs when it doesn't.
Write `print("Shield up.")` on a new line under line 3, with four spaces in front.

exercises.title: Colon and indent
exercises.martu:
Two marks make an `if` work, and you know both from English class. A [[colon]] introduces a list, and in an outline, sub-points are indented under their main point. In Python, the colon at the end of `if mana < 6:` says: here come its steps. The [[indent]], four spaces, says: this line belongs to the `if`.
This code has three [[bug|bugs]] (mistakes in code). Two are loud: Python stops and shows an error, one at a time. Read each error box in the Console: its title first, then Python's last line, then the line number. The third bug is quiet: the code runs, but one line is in the wrong place.
*Mend* means fix. Each step below starts with it.

anotherWay.label: Colon, then indent
anotherWay.text:
1. The colon says: here come the `if`'s steps.
2. The indent says: this line belongs to the `if`.
3. The first line with no indent is not part of the `if`. It runs every time.

anotherWay.label: Which lines belong?
anotherWay.text:
```text
if hours_left < 3:
    print("Shield up.")
print("The clock ticks on.")
```
`print("Shield up.")` is indented, so it belongs to the `if`. It runs only when the answer is `True`.
`print("The clock ticks on.")` has no indent, so it is not part of the `if`. It runs every time.
Every `if` line ends with `:`. Each line that belongs to it starts with four spaces. A line with no spaces runs every time.

exercises.martu:
[[else]] means *otherwise*. It has no question of its own. Its lines run when the `if` answer was `False`. In plain English: *If it rains, take a coat. Otherwise, take sunglasses.* You never take both. In Python, `else:` goes on its own line, right under the `if`'s indented lines.

exercises.title: Clock colors
exercises.martu:
[[elif]] is short for *else, if*: another question, asked only when the questions above it were `False`, like `elif hours_left <= 12:`. Python checks the chain from the top, takes the *first* question that is `True`, and skips the rest. It's like a grading scale: 90 or more is an A, 80 or more is a B. Check *80 or more* first, and a 95 gets a B. Order matters.
Each path through the chain is a [[branch]]: the lines under the `if`, under one `elif`, or under the `else`.
My Ley Clock should glow red at 2 hours or fewer, bright blue up to 12, and calm blue after that. This chain is in the wrong order. Which hours get the wrong color?

anotherWay.label: A hall of doors
anotherWay.text: Picture a hall of doors. You try them from the front, and you walk through the first one that opens. A door further back never gets tried, even if it would open too.

anotherWay.label: The chain, top to bottom
anotherWay.text:
```text
<= 2 ?   yes -> red          (stop)
  no
<= 12 ?  yes -> bright blue  (stop)
  no
else         -> calm blue
```

anotherWay.label: Trace 2, 7 and 20
anotherWay.text:
In the fixed chain:
1. 2 hours: `2 <= 2` is `True`. Red. Stop.
2. 7 hours: `7 <= 2` is `False`. `7 <= 12` is `True`. Bright blue. Stop.
3. 20 hours: both are `False`, so the `else` runs: calm blue.
The first true branch wins. So first, the question that lets the fewest numbers through: `<= 2`, then `<= 12`, then `else`.

exercises.title: And, or, not
exercises.martu:
Three small words join yes-or-no questions. They work like *and*, *or* and *not* in an English sentence: *You may leave when your work is done and your desk is clean*. In Python, `mana >= cost and affinity >= required` is `True` only when both questions are `True`.
[[and]]: both answers must be `True`. To cast, Oogrish needs enough mana (magic power) and enough affinity (how strong his magic is).
[[or]]: one `True` is enough, and two are fine too. Lucky passes if his first roll or his second roll is high enough.
[[not]]: flips the answer. `not True` is `False`.

anotherWay.label: Work it out with the real numbers
anotherWay.text:
Oogrish: mana 12, cost 9, affinity 9, needs 9.
1. `mana >= cost`: 12 >= 9, `True`.
2. `affinity >= required`: 9 >= 9, `True`.
3. `True and True` is `True`. He casts.
With only 5 mana: `False and True` is `False`. With `or`, it would be `True`, and he would cast without enough mana. Bad.

anotherWay.label: Keys
anotherWay.text: `and` is a door with two locks: you need both keys. `or` is two doors: either key gets you in.

anotherWay.label: Two lamps
anotherWay.text:
```text
and: [on]  [on]  -> on
and: [on]  [off] -> off
or:  [on]  [off] -> on
or:  [off] [off] -> off
not: [on]        -> off
```
`and` needs both. `or` needs at least one. `not` flips the answer.

exercises.title: Roll a die
exercises.martu:
A fair die can land on any of its faces, and every face is equally likely. Python can roll one. [[import]] `random` brings in Python's dice, like fetching the dice bin from the shelf, once, at the top. Then `random.randint(1, 6)` ([[randint]]) rolls a d6, a die with 6 faces: it gives a whole number from 1 to 6, *both ends included*. So 1 and 6 can come up. 0 and 7 never do.
Here, *random* doesn't mean weird. It means every face has the same chance.
Press Run a few times and watch the numbers change. Then fix the two dice.

anotherWay.text:

```text
d6:  [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6]
      ^ low            ^ high
random.randint(1, 6)
```

2. Go to the line number it gives, and fix that line.

items.title: Match: Another Way to Choose
items.summary: The four-answers chain, written with `match` and `case`. Learn to read both.
items.body:
There is another way to write the four-answers chain. It is called [[match]].
`match choice:` says: look at what is in `choice`. Each `case "option 1":` says: if it is these exact letters, run the indented lines under me. `case _:` catches anything else, like `else`.
Python tries the cases from the top and runs the first one that fits. Then it stops, the same as an `if` and `elif` chain.
The two examples below show the same line. Press Run on both and compare them.
The campaign uses `elif`, so learn to read both. When you write your own code, use whichever one is clearer to you.

code: print("The decay? The clock is speeding up.")
print("It turned red once. Never again, I hope.")

exercises.title: A fifth option
exercises.martu:
Here is the four-answers chain written with `match`. Each `case "option 1":` line works like an `if` or `elif` line, and `case _:` at the end catches anything else, like `else`.
A fifth option appeared on the board. Give it a `case` of its own.

anotherWay.label: match next to elif
anotherWay.text:
With `elif`:
```text
if choice == "option 1":
elif choice == "option 2":
else:
```
With `match`:
```text
match choice:
    case "option 1":
    case "option 2":
    case _:
```
The same choices, written two ways. Each `if` or `elif` line becomes a `case` line, and `else:` becomes `case _:`.

anotherWay.text:

2. Right above it, add `case "option 5":`.
3. Under that, indented once more, add `mar_tu_says("...")`.

items.title: Ley Clock Quiz
items.summary: Quiz: 8 questions on comparisons, `if` / `elif` / `else`, `and` / `or`, and dice. Retake it as often as you like.

questions.q: What will this code show in the Console?
questions.explain: `>=` means *at least*: 12 is at least 12, so `True`. `>` means *more than*, and 12 is not more than 12, so `False`. On a number line, `>=` is the filled dot: the number itself counts.

questions.q: What will this code show in the Console?
questions.explain: `2 <= 2` is `True`, so the first branch runs, and Python skips the rest. Only one branch of a chain ever runs.

questions.q: Which whole numbers can `random.randint(1, 6)` give?

whyWrong.0: `randint` starts at the first number you give it: 1, not 0. And 6 can come up too.
whyWrong.1: `randint` includes both ends, so 6 can come up.
whyWrong.3: 0 is below the first number, so it never comes up.

questions.explain: `random.randint(1, 6)` gives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6. Both ends are included, like the faces of a real d6.

questions.q: What will this code show in the Console?
questions.explain: There is enough mana (12 >= 9), but affinity 8 is below 9. `and` needs both answers `True`, so the answer is `False`.

questions.q: Put the lines in order, with their indents, so the code shows Mar'tu's reply to option 2.
lines: print("The decay? The clock is speeding up.")
print("It turned red once. Never again, I hope.")
questions.expectedOutput: The decay? The clock is speeding up.
questions.explain: One `if`, then the `elif` lines, in order. Each option is text, so it keeps its quotes.

questions.q: This code should show `A perfect roll!` for a 20, but Python stops with an error. Fix it.
questions.explain: `=` puts a value in a box. An `if` asks a question, so it needs `==`: is the same as.

questions.q: Which line asks whether the box `hero` holds the text Lucky?

whyWrong.0: `=` puts Lucky in the box. It doesn't ask anything.
whyWrong.2: With no quotes, Python looks for a box named `Lucky`. The name is text, so it needs quotes.
whyWrong.3: With quotes, `"hero"` is the word hero, not the box. That asks whether two different words match.

questions.explain: `hero == "Lucky"` asks: is the text in the box `hero` the same as these exact letters?

questions.q: What will this code show in the Console?
choices:
A good roll.
A great roll.
questions.explain: `18 >= 10` is `True`, so the first branch wins and Python skips the rest, even though 18 is also great. The order rule: first, the question that lets the fewest numbers through. `>= 15` lets fewer numbers through than `>= 10`, so it should go first.

items.title: Road Encounter Table
items.summary: Roll a d20 (a die with 20 faces), and an `if` / `elif` / `else` table picks what happens on the road to the old Institute. You write what happens.
items.intro:
The road to the old Institute is long. Oogrish wants an encounter table: you roll a d20 (a die with 20 faces), and the table says what happens on the road. You write what happens.
Three parts, in order: A. Roll the die. B. Fill in the table. C. Show the result.
The table has five tiers (rows), one for each group of rolls: 1, then 2 to 6, 7 to 15, 16 to 19, and 20. The first two branches are already in your code. Use any words you like for each tier.
items.martu:
An encounter table is a chain of `if`, `elif` and `else`, like a grading scale: check from the top, and the first tier that fits wins. So `elif road_roll <= 6:` catches 2 to 6, because the 1 was already caught above it.
Oogrish is right, as usual. Roll first, then let the table decide, then show the result.
I test your code with my own rolls, one for every tier, so I can see each one. Your words stay yours.

anotherWay.label: The table
anotherWay.text:
```text
roll 1        -> tier 1
roll 2 to 6   -> tier 2
roll 7 to 15  -> tier 3
roll 16 to 19 -> tier 4
roll 20       -> tier 5
```
Each tier is one branch of the chain.

anotherWay.label: Trace a 6 and a 7
anotherWay.text:
1. A 6: `6 == 1`? No. `6 <= 6`? Yes: the ley-line tier. Stop.
2. A 7: `7 == 1`? No. `7 <= 6`? No. `7 <= 15`? Yes: the quiet road. Stop.

anotherWay.label: Oogrish's table
anotherWay.text: Oogrish keeps his tables on the back of a map, one tier per line, starting from the 1. The 20 is everything the other tiers didn't catch, so it is the `else`.

bonus.title: Dumb Luck and a sharp eye
bonus.text:
Lucky wants two things.
1. Dumb Luck: right after the first roll, if `road_roll` is 1, roll it once more. Only once.
2. A perception check (does Lucky spot something?): make `night_time = True` and `perception_roll = 14`. Then make a box `spotted` that is `True` only when `perception_roll` is at least 12 and it is not night time.
hints: Dumb Luck goes right after the first roll: an `if` asks whether `road_roll` is 1, with a new roll under it, indented. The perception check is one line with `and` and `not`.

items.title: Three Roads to the Institute
items.summary: Walk, ride Gearshift's jeep, or jump with Lucky's Telegun? Work out what each road costs, then let your code pick the cheapest.
items.intro:
Mar'tu needs brass instruments from the old Institute. There are three ways to get there, and every cost is counted in coins:
1. On foot: the party packs glug, Lucky's drink, for the road. A longer walk needs more.
2. Gearshift's jeep form: 2 coins of starlode (his fuel) for each mile, plus 5 coins to start.
3. Lucky's Telegun, which jumps the party there: free on a roll of 15 or more. Under 15, Lucky lands in a hedge, and you walk anyway. Again.
Nobody agrees how far it is. So your code must pick the cheapest road for any `distance` (the miles). The prices are in the notes in your code, under `# A.`, `# B.` and `# C.`
items.martu:
This project has five parts, A to E. Each part has a note in your code, like `# A. Rations on foot`, and the list under Your tasks uses the same letters. First work out what each road costs. Then an `if` / `elif` / `else` picks the cheapest.
Build every cost from the boxes, like a formula in math class: area = length × width works for any rectangle, but the answer 12 fits only one. I test your code with other distances and other rolls.
I counted everything in coins. Starlode, glug, hedges. Everything.

anotherWay.label: The three roads, side by side
anotherWay.text:
What each road costs, in coins, when the Telegun roll is under 15 (a hedge):
```text
miles  walk  jeep  Telegun
  5      8    15     18
 30     70    65     80
 80    150   165    160
```
On a roll of 15 or more, the Telegun costs 0, so it is the cheapest every time.

anotherWay.label: One part at a time
anotherWay.text:
1. A: three prices, so `if`, `elif`, `else`. Put first the question that lets the fewest numbers through.
2. B: one line, worked out from `distance`.
3. C: roll the die, then an `if` / `else` on the roll.
4. D: ask *is walking the cheapest?*, then *is the jeep cheaper than the Telegun?*, then `else`.
5. E: glue `road` and `str(cost)` into one line with `+`.

anotherWay.label: You've seen this
anotherWay.text: In the game, `cast_spell` held the barrier by picking one of three paths: not skilled enough, not enough mana, or cast. Python checked from the top and took the first true branch. Your road picker works the same way.

items.title: When Spells Fizzle: Reading Errors
items.summary: Read Python's error messages like Mar'tu does, find the line, and fix it. No error but a wrong answer? Print the values.

exercises.title: Anatomy of a fizzle
exercises.martu:
When a spell *fizzles*, it fails, and Python stops with an error. In the box in the Console, Show Python's full message opens Python's whole note: a [[traceback]]. Like a teacher's note in the margin, it points to the spot. In the game it's all you get. Read it from the bottom up.
1. The last line: the error's name, then what went wrong, like `NameError: name 'lantren' is not defined`.
2. Higher up, `line` and a number: where Python stopped.
3. Inside the little `'` marks: the name Python could not find.
Press Run. While the message is on screen, copy the three parts into the boxes at the bottom. Then put `#` at the start of line 4 and press Run again.

anotherWay.label: The message, part by part
anotherWay.text:
1. The last line, read it first: `NameError: name 'mana_cost' is not defined`. Its first word, `NameError`, is the error's name.
2. Higher up: `File "main.py", line 4`. That is the line where Python stopped.
3. Inside the little `'` marks: `mana_cost`, the name Python could not find.

anotherWay.label: Where to look, in order
anotherWay.text:
1. In the box in the Console, read the title, then Python's last line: the error's name, then what went wrong.
2. Find the line number, and go to that line in your code.
3. On that line, find the name or mark the message talks about.

anotherWay.label: A note on the door
anotherWay.text: It is like a note from a delivery driver: *Could not deliver to line 4: nobody called mana_cost lives here.* The driver is not angry. The note says where, and what was missing.
Last line: the error's name and the missing name. Full message: the line number.

exercises.martu:
This [[bug]] is quiet: the code runs with no error, but the answer is wrong. It's like spell-check, which won't catch *their* for *there*. With no error to read, make Python show you the values, like `print(mana)`. It's the same as showing your work in math class: each step on paper shows where it went wrong.

anotherWay.label: Why printing the values works
anotherWay.text: Printing the values is a real way to find bugs, and programmers use it every day. When the code runs but the answer is wrong, the values tell you which line to doubt.

anotherWay.label: Hunt a quiet bug
anotherWay.text:

2. Do the question by hand: is 9 > 9? No.
3. Should it be yes? Exactly enough should cast. So the sign is the bug.

exercises.martu:
You've met [[bug|bugs]] before: a loud bug stops Python with an error, and a quiet bug runs but gives a wrong answer. I hunt both with the same four steps every time, the way you proofread an essay one mark at a time.
1. Read the box in the Console: its title, then Python's last line.
2. Find the line number, and go to that line.
3. Check the line above it too, and the lines where its boxes were made.
4. No error, but a wrong answer? Print the values.

exercises.title: Lines Python can't read
exercises.martu:
*Syntax* is how a line is put together, like grammar in English class. A [[SyntaxError]] means Python can't read a line, so it stops before anything runs. This spell has three: a missing `"`, a missing `:` and a missing `)`.
Guess first: three mistakes, so how many error boxes will you see? Press Run and count.
Then fix them one at a time. After each fix, press Run and read the new box. A new error means Python got further.

anotherWay.label: Why only one error box?
anotherWay.text: Python reads all of your code before it runs any of it. It stops at the first line it can't read, so it never gets to the other mistakes. Fix that one, press Run again, and it shows you the next. That is why errors come one at a time.

anotherWay.label: Python reads, then runs
anotherWay.text:
```text
Python reads every line.
Stuck on line 2?
  -> stop: one error box.
All fine?
  -> run the code.
```
With a SyntaxError, nothing runs at all. Not even line 1.

1. Press Run.
2. Read the box: its title, then Python's last line.
3. Fix that one mistake.
4. Press Run again. A new error means Python got further.
Quotes in pairs. A colon after `if`. Parentheses in pairs.

exercises.title: Names Python can't find
exercises.martu:
A [[NameError]] means Python met a name that no line has made yet. It's like a story that says *she grabbed it* but never said who *she* is. `print(mama)` stops Python if no line made `mama`.
This spell has four, each for a different reason: a typo, a box used too early, words without quotes, and a capital letter. Read the box each time. Sometimes Python even asks: *Did you mean ...?*

anotherWay.label: Four ways to lose a name
anotherWay.text:
```text
mama      a typo
shield    used too early
Fireball  words, no quotes
health    made as Health
```

1. Read Python's last line: which name?
2. Look through your code for that name, letter for letter.
3. No line makes it? Make it first, fix the spelling, or add quotes if you meant words.
Not defined? Check the spelling, the capitals, the order, and the quotes.

items.title: Mar'tu's Seal
items.summary: An `assert` line says what must be true. Put one at the boundary, the exact number that should pass, and a quiet bug becomes loud.
items.body:
A seal is an [[assert]] line: the word `assert`, then a yes-or-no question whose answer must be `True`. It's like checking a math answer by putting it back into the equation. `assert passed == True` says: `passed` must be `True` here.
If the answer is `True`, nothing happens, and your code goes on. If it is `False`, Python stops with `AssertionError` and gives the line:
```text
File "main.py", line 4
    assert passed == True
AssertionError
```
Why bother? Seals catch quiet [[bug|bugs]]. A `>` where `>=` belongs gives no error at all. A seal at the *boundary*, the exact number that should still pass, turns that quiet bug into a loud one.
At the Institute we sealed our work this way. The campaign never asks for seals. They are for the careful, yes?

exercises.title: Seal the check
exercises.martu:
Your code tries three rolls against a `needed` of 15: 14, then exactly 15, then 16. Under each `# seal:` note, write an `assert` that says what `passed` must be for that roll, like `assert passed == True`.
Then I test your seals: I break a copy of your `passed` lines on purpose. Good seals notice.

anotherWay.label: Three seals on a number line
anotherWay.text:
```text
   14        15        16
   fail  |  pass      pass
   ^          ^          ^
 False     True       True
```
The seal at exactly 15 is the one that catches a `>`.

anotherWay.label: Why does this work?
anotherWay.text: `>` instead of `>=` gives no error: a quiet bug. A seal at the boundary, the exact number that should still pass, says what must be true. When it is not, Python stops. The quiet bug becomes a loud one.
Below: `False`. Exactly: `True`. Above: `True`.

items.title: Quick Check 2 · Form A questions
items.summary: Four questions that go with Quick Check 2. To pass the Quick Check, get 3 of the 4 right.

questions.q: What will this print?
questions.explain: `>=` means *at least*. 11 is not at least 12, but 12 is, and so is 13. Exactly enough passes.

questions.q: What will this print?
questions.explain: 18 is at least 15, so the first branch runs, and Python skips the rest. 18 is also at least 10, but only the first true branch runs. With 12 it would print `A hit.`, and with 4, `A miss.`

questions.q: Which values can `random.randint(1, 8)` give?

whyWrong.0: `randint` starts at the first number you give it: 1, not 0.
whyWrong.1: `randint` includes both ends, so 8 can come up too.
whyWrong.3: Both ends are included: 1 and 8. A d8 has no 0.

questions.explain: `random.randint(1, 8)` is a d8: any whole number from 1 to 8, both ends included.

questions.q: What will this print?
questions.explain: `mana >= cost` is True, but `affinity >= required` is False: 9 is not at least 10. `and` needs both, so the part in parentheses gives False. `not` flips it: True. Oogrish can't cast this one yet.

items.summary: Four questions that go with Quick Check 2. To pass the Quick Check, get 3 of the 4 right.

questions.q: What will this print?
questions.explain: `<=` means *at most*. 1 and 2 are at most 2; 3 is not. Exactly 2 counts.

questions.q: What will this print?
questions.explain: 2 is at most 2, so the first branch runs, and Python skips the rest. 2 is also at most 12, but only the first true branch runs. With 12 it would print `bright blue`, and with 40, `calm blue`.

questions.q: Which values can `random.randint(1, 12)` give?

whyWrong.0: `randint` starts at the first number you give it: 1, not 0.
whyWrong.1: `randint` includes both ends, so 12 can come up too.
whyWrong.3: Both ends are included: 1 and 12. A d12 has no 0.

questions.explain: `random.randint(1, 12)` is a d12: any whole number from 1 to 12, both ends included.

questions.q: What will this print?
questions.explain: `mana >= cost` is False: 26 is not at least 30. `affinity >= required` is True. `and` needs both, so the part in parentheses gives False. `not` flips it: True. Lucky is 4 mana short.

entries.note: No quotes: `True` and `False` are Python's yes and no. (Lesson: True or False, Yes?)
Read `=` as *gets* and `==` as *is the same as*. Every letter, space and capital counts.
`!=` means *is not the same as*. `<` is less than, `>` is more than, `<=` is at most, and `>=` is at least.
On a number line, `>` is the open dot: the number itself is left out. `>=` is the filled dot, so exactly enough still passes.
`answer.lower()` gives a small-letter copy, so capitals stop mattering. Alone on a line, the copy is thrown away: keep it with `answer = answer.lower()`.
The colon says *here come its steps*. The lines under it, indented 4 spaces, belong to the `if`, like sub-points in an outline. (Lesson: If the Clock Turns Red)
`else:` has no question. It runs when the `if` did not.
Python checks from the top and runs only the first true branch, like a grading scale. So put first the question that lets the fewest numbers through. `else` is always last.
`and` needs both answers True. `or` needs at least one. `not` flips the answer.
`import random` once, at the top. `random.randint(1, 20)` gives 1 to 20, both ends included.
